questions.title: ApplicationContext vs BeanFactory
questions.question: What is the difference between ApplicationContext and BeanFactory?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- **`BeanFactory`:** the basic IoC container — creates and wires beans
- **`ApplicationContext`:** extends `BeanFactory` with enterprise features
- **What AC adds:** event publishing, internationalization, AOP, resource loading, lifecycle management
- **`BeanFactory` is lazy by default, `ApplicationContext` is eager:** singletons created at startup
- **Red flag:** thinking they're interchangeable — `ApplicationContext` is what you always use in Spring Boot

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
`BeanFactory` is Spring's basic IoC container interface — it creates beans, manages dependencies, and provides bean retrieval. `ApplicationContext` extends `BeanFactory` and adds enterprise-level features.

The additions in `ApplicationContext` include event publishing via `ApplicationEventPublisher`, resource loading via `ResourceLoader`, internationalization support, automatic `BeanPostProcessor` registration, and automatic `BeanFactoryPostProcessor` registration. Most importantly, `ApplicationContext` eagerly creates all singleton beans at startup, which catches configuration errors immediately.

`BeanFactory` creates beans lazily — only when first requested. In practice, nobody uses `BeanFactory` directly in application code. Spring Boot's `SpringApplication` always creates an `ApplicationContext`. `BeanFactory` awareness is useful for understanding Spring internals.

sections.title: Why You Never Use BeanFactory Directly — Even Though It Does Most of the Work
sections.content:
`BeanFactory` is the core container in Spring — it creates beans, resolves dependencies, and manages the singleton cache. `ApplicationContext` extends `BeanFactory` and adds everything else: event publishing, internationalization, resource loading, environment abstraction, and automatic registration of `BeanPostProcessors`. In practice, you always use `ApplicationContext` because `BeanFactory` alone is missing the features that make Spring useful.

The relationship is inheritance, not delegation. `ApplicationContext` **is a** `BeanFactory` (it extends the interface). Every `ApplicationContext` implementation contains a `DefaultListableBeanFactory` internally that does the actual bean management. The context adds layers on top: it scans for `@Component` classes, processes `@Configuration`, publishes lifecycle events, and registers all the `BeanPostProcessor` beans that enable features like `@Autowired` and `@Transactional`.

The practical difference matters when writing framework code or tests. `BeanFactory` is lazy — it creates beans only when requested via `getBean()`. `ApplicationContext` is eager — it pre-instantiates all singleton beans during `refresh()`. This means `ApplicationContext` catches configuration errors at startup (missing dependencies, circular references), while `BeanFactory` defers them to first access.

The most common mistake is thinking you need to choose between them. You don't. `@SpringBootApplication` creates an `ApplicationContext`, and that's what every production application uses. `BeanFactory` is an implementation detail you interact with only when building custom framework extensions like `BeanFactoryPostProcessor`.

sections.title: BeanFactory vs. ApplicationContext: Feature and Behavior Differences
sections.content:
The comparison reveals that `BeanFactory` handles core bean management, while `ApplicationContext` adds the features that make a production application viable.

| Feature | BeanFactory | ApplicationContext |
|---|---|---|
| Bean creation and DI | Yes | Yes (delegates to internal BeanFactory) |
| Singleton caching | Yes | Yes |
| Bean scopes | Singleton and prototype only | All scopes (request, session, etc.) |
| BeanPostProcessor registration | Manual — you must register them yourself | Automatic — detects and registers all BPPs |
| Event publishing | No | Yes — `ApplicationEventPublisher` |
| Internationalization (i18n) | No | Yes — `MessageSource` |
| Resource loading | No | Yes — `ResourceLoader` |
| Environment and profiles | No | Yes — `Environment` abstraction |
| Eager initialization | No — lazy by default | Yes — pre-instantiates singletons |
| @Autowired support | Only if you manually register the BPP | Automatic |

The "BeanPostProcessor registration" row is the critical difference. Without automatic BPP registration, `@Autowired` doesn't work, `@Transactional` proxies aren't created, and `@Value` properties aren't resolved. A plain `BeanFactory` requires you to register these processors manually — which is why nobody uses `BeanFactory` directly in application code.

questions.title: BeanDefinition
questions.question: What is a BeanDefinition in Spring?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- **Metadata recipe, not an instance:** describes how to create the bean
- **Contains:** class, scope, constructor args, property values, init/destroy methods
- **Read from:** `@Component` annotations, `@Bean` methods, XML config
- **`BeanDefinitionRegistry`:** where definitions are registered before beans are created
- **Red flag:** confusing `BeanDefinition` (metadata) with the bean instance itself

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
A `BeanDefinition` is metadata that describes how Spring should create a bean — it's a recipe, not the bean itself. It contains the bean class, scope, constructor arguments, property values, initialization and destroy methods, lazy/eager flag, and dependency declarations.

During the context startup's `refresh()` phase, Spring scans your annotations and `@Configuration` classes, creating `BeanDefinition` objects for each bean it discovers. These definitions are registered in the `BeanDefinitionRegistry`. Only later, during `finishBeanFactoryInitialization`, does Spring actually instantiate the beans from these definitions.

This two-phase approach is what `BeanFactoryPostProcessor` exploits — it runs between definition registration and instantiation, allowing you to modify definitions before any beans are created. `PropertySourcesPlaceholderConfigurer` reads `${property.key}` placeholders from definitions and replaces them with actual values.

sections.title: The Blueprint Object That Exists Before Any Bean Instance Is Created
sections.content:
A `BeanDefinition` is Spring's internal representation of a bean — its **metadata**, not its instance. It describes what class to instantiate, what scope to use, which constructor to call, what dependencies to inject, and which init/destroy methods to invoke. Think of it as a blueprint: Spring collects all the blueprints first, then builds objects from them.

This separation between definition and instance is fundamental to Spring's extensibility. `BeanFactoryPostProcessor` implementations can modify bean definitions **before** any instance is created — changing a bean's scope, adding property values, or even registering entirely new definitions. This is how `PropertySourcesPlaceholderConfigurer` works: it walks every bean definition, finds `${...}` placeholders in property values, and replaces them with resolved values before any bean is instantiated.

Every mechanism that registers beans — `@Component` scanning, `@Bean` methods, XML declarations, `@Import` — ultimately creates a `BeanDefinition` and registers it with the `BeanDefinitionRegistry`. The specific subclass varies: `@Component` scanning creates `ScannedGenericBeanDefinition`, `@Bean` methods create `ConfigurationClassBeanDefinition`, and XML creates `GenericBeanDefinition`. But they all implement the same `BeanDefinition` interface.

Understanding bean definitions helps debug startup issues. When you see "No qualifying bean of type X," the question is whether a `BeanDefinition` for X exists (it wasn't scanned or registered) or whether the definition exists but instantiation failed (a dependency is missing or a condition failed).

questions.title: Spring Event System
questions.question: How does Spring's event publishing and listening system work?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- **Publisher/subscriber within the Spring context:** decouples event source from listeners
- **`ApplicationEventPublisher`:** inject and call `publishEvent()` to publish
- **`@EventListener`:** annotation for receiving events — method signature determines event type
- **Synchronous by default:** same thread, same transaction
- **Red flag:** not knowing events are synchronous by default — shows lack of practical usage

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
Spring's event system implements the observer pattern within the application context. Components publish events by calling `ApplicationEventPublisher.publishEvent()`, and listeners receive them via `@EventListener` methods. The event type is determined by the method parameter — Spring routes events to listeners whose parameter type matches.

By default, events are synchronous — the publisher's thread executes all listeners before `publishEvent()` returns. This means listeners share the publisher's transaction, which is important: if a listener throws an exception, it can roll back the publisher's transaction.

For async event handling, annotate the listener with `@Async`. For events that should only fire after a transaction commits, use `@TransactionalEventListener(phase = AFTER_COMMIT)`. This prevents sending a confirmation email when the database transaction later rolls back.

sections.title: How Spring's Event Bus Decouples Components Without Message Brokers
sections.content:
Spring's event system is an in-process publish-subscribe mechanism. A publisher sends an event, and every registered listener for that event type is notified. Unlike external message brokers (Kafka, RabbitMQ), this is purely in-memory — events don't survive application restarts and can't cross JVM boundaries.

The value isn't distributed messaging — it's **architectural decoupling within a single application**. When `OrderService` publishes an `OrderPlacedEvent`, it doesn't know that `InventoryService`, `NotificationService`, and `AnalyticsService` are listening. Adding a fourth listener doesn't require changing `OrderService`. Removing one doesn't leave a broken dependency. Each concern reacts independently.

Events are synchronous by default: `publishEvent()` calls each listener sequentially on the same thread, in the same transaction. This is important — a listener that throws an exception can roll back the publisher's transaction, and a slow listener blocks the publisher until it finishes. For truly async behavior, annotate the listener with `@Async`, but be aware that async listeners lose the transactional context.

The event system is built on `ApplicationEventMulticaster`, which maintains a list of listeners and dispatches events by type. Spring auto-configures a `SimpleApplicationEventMulticaster` that handles synchronous dispatch. You can replace it with a custom multicaster for async dispatch, error handling, or event filtering — but the default is sufficient for most applications.

questions.title: Spring Resource Loading
questions.question: How does Spring's Resource abstraction work?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- **`Resource` interface:** abstracts over classpath, file system, URL, ServletContext resources
- **Prefixes:** `classpath:`, `file:`, `http://`, `classpath*:`
- **`ResourceLoader`:** inject to resolve resources programmatically
- **`@Value("classpath:...")` for injection:** common way to inject a resource
- **Red flag:** using `getClass().getClassLoader().getResourceAsStream()` when Spring's `Resource` is available

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
Spring's `Resource` interface provides a uniform way to access resources regardless of where they're stored — classpath, file system, HTTP URL, or Servlet context. This abstraction means your code doesn't change whether you're loading from the classpath in tests or from a file system path in production.

The prefix in the resource path determines the type: `classpath:` for classpath resources (inside the JAR), `file:` for file system paths, `http://` for HTTP resources. `classpath*:` is special — it finds all matching resources on the classpath, useful for loading configuration from multiple JARs.

You access resources by injecting `ResourceLoader` and calling `getResource("classpath:data/config.json")`, or by using `@Value("classpath:config.json") Resource resource` to directly inject a specific resource.

sections.title: The Abstraction That Makes 'Where the File Lives' Irrelevant to Your Code
sections.content:
Spring's `Resource` interface abstracts away the physical location of files. Whether your template lives on the classpath, the filesystem, a URL, or inside a JAR, the same API reads it. Your code calls `resource.getInputStream()` without knowing or caring about the source — and when deployment changes from an exploded directory to a fat JAR, nothing in your code breaks.

Without this abstraction, you'd use `File` for filesystem paths, `ClassLoader.getResourceAsStream()` for classpath resources, and `URL.openStream()` for remote resources. Each has different APIs, different error handling, and different behavior in different deployment environments. A `File` path that works in development (`/src/main/resources/template.html`) breaks in a JAR because resources inside JARs aren't files — they're ZIP entries.

`ResourceLoader` is the interface that resolves resource paths to `Resource` objects. Every `ApplicationContext` is a `ResourceLoader`, so you can inject it anywhere. The path prefix determines the resolution strategy: `classpath:` looks in the classpath, `file:` looks in the filesystem, `https:` fetches from a URL. No prefix defaults to the context type — a `ClassPathXmlApplicationContext` defaults to classpath, a `FileSystemXmlApplicationContext` defaults to filesystem.

The most common mistake is using `new File("config.json")` inside a Spring Boot application packaged as a JAR. This fails because the file is inside the JAR, not on the filesystem. Using `resourceLoader.getResource("classpath:config.json")` works in both development (exploded classes) and production (fat JAR).

questions.title: Spring Environment
questions.question: What is the Spring Environment abstraction?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- **Two aspects:** active profiles + property sources
- **`PropertySources`:** ordered list of property source — higher priority sources override lower
- **Property source order:** system properties > env vars > `application.properties`
- **`@PropertySource`:** add a custom properties file to the environment
- **Red flag:** not knowing the `Environment` unified profile and property management

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
The `Environment` interface is Spring's unified abstraction over two concerns: active profiles and property sources. It lets you query both — which profiles are active and what value a property has — through a single object.

Property sources are layered in priority order. System properties — set with `-Dkey=value` on the JVM command line — have higher priority than environment variables, which have higher priority than `application.properties`. Profile-specific files like `application-prod.properties` have higher priority than the base `application.properties`. Command-line arguments have the highest priority.

When you call `environment.getProperty("key")`, Spring walks through the property sources in priority order and returns the first value it finds. This is exactly how Spring Boot's property resolution works — `@Value` and `@ConfigurationProperties` both delegate to the `Environment`.

sections.title: The Unified API That Merges Properties From 17 Different Sources
sections.content:
Spring's `Environment` abstraction solves a problem that every non-trivial application faces: configuration values come from many sources — `application.properties`, `application.yml`, environment variables, system properties, command-line arguments, Spring Cloud Config, Vault, and more. Without a unified API, your code would need to check each source manually, handle priority conflicts, and parse different formats.

`Environment` merges all these sources into a single ordered list called **property sources**. When you call `environment.getProperty("db.url")`, Spring walks the list from highest to lowest priority and returns the first match. The priority order is fixed: command-line arguments override environment variables, which override `application.properties`, which override defaults. This is why setting `SERVER_PORT=9090` as an environment variable overrides `server.port=8080` in your properties file.

The `Environment` also manages **profiles** — named groups of configuration that activate based on deployment context. `@Profile("production")` on a bean means it's only created when the "production" profile is active. Profile-specific property files (`application-production.properties`) are loaded only when their profile is active, and their values override the base `application.properties`.

The practical value is that the same application artifact runs in every environment — development, staging, production — with behavior controlled entirely by external configuration. No recompilation, no different builds, no environment-specific branches. This is a core principle of twelve-factor applications, and Spring's `Environment` makes it nearly effortless.

questions.title: Spring Expression Language (SpEL)
questions.question: What is Spring Expression Language (SpEL) and where is it used?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- **Powerful expression language:** supports method calls, arithmetic, conditionals, collection projection
- **`#{...}` syntax:** distinguishes SpEL from `${property}` substitution
- **Used in:** `@Value`, `@Cacheable` key, `@PreAuthorize`, `@ConditionalOn*`, `@EventListener` condition
- **Bean references with `@bean`:** access another bean's property
- **Red flag:** confusing `#{SpEL}` with `${property.placeholder}` — different mechanisms

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
Spring Expression Language — SpEL — is a powerful expression language embedded in the Spring Framework. It uses the `#{...}` syntax to distinguish it from property placeholder `${...}` substitution. While `${property.key}` just looks up a property value, SpEL can execute method calls, evaluate conditions, navigate object graphs, filter collections, and perform arithmetic.

SpEL appears in several Spring annotations. In `@Value`, `#{T(Math).random()}` calls a static method. In `@Cacheable(key = "#id")`, `#id` references the method parameter. In Spring Security's `@PreAuthorize("#user.email == authentication.name")`, it evaluates access rules. In `@ConditionalOnExpression`, it evaluates complex startup conditions.

In practice, you use SpEL most often for `@Cacheable` key expressions and `@PreAuthorize` security rules.

sections.title: The Embedded Language That Powers @Value, @Cacheable, and Spring Security Expressions
sections.content:
Spring Expression Language (SpEL) is an expression language embedded throughout the Spring framework. You've used it — even if you didn't realize it — every time you wrote a `@Value("#{ ... }")` annotation, a `@Cacheable(key = "#user.id")` expression, or a `@PreAuthorize("hasRole('ADMIN')")` security check. Each of these is a SpEL expression evaluated at runtime.

SpEL is more powerful than simple property resolution (`${...}`). It can access object properties, call methods, perform arithmetic, evaluate boolean logic, work with collections (filtering, projection), create objects, and reference Spring beans. This power makes it invaluable for declarative configuration — but it also makes it a source of subtle bugs when expressions fail at runtime instead of compile time.

The key distinction is between **`${...}`** and **`#{...}`** syntax. `${property.key}` is a property placeholder — it resolves to a value from `application.properties` or environment variables. `#{expression}` is a SpEL expression — it evaluates Java-like logic at runtime. You can nest them: `#{'${list.property}'.split(',')}` resolves the property first, then applies SpEL to split it into a list.

The most common SpEL mistake is using it where a simpler mechanism works. `@Value("#{systemProperties['java.version']}")` does the same thing as `@Value("${java.version}")` — but the property placeholder is simpler, faster, and has better IDE support. Use SpEL only when you need its expression capabilities: method calls, collection operations, conditional logic, or bean references.

sections.title: Where SpEL Appears: The Six Most Common Integration Points
sections.content:
SpEL is embedded in different annotations across the framework, and the **evaluation context** differs in each. Understanding what's available in each context prevents "property not found" and "method not resolved" errors.

**1. `@Value("#{...}")`** — Evaluated during bean creation. Can access system properties, environment beans, and other Spring beans via `@beanName.method()`.

```java
@Value("#{@configService.getDefaultTimeout()}")
private int timeout;
```

**2. `@Cacheable(key = "...")`** — Evaluated on each method call. Has access to method parameters via `#paramName`, the return value via `#result` (in `@CachePut`), and the root object with metadata like `#root.methodName`.

**3. `@PreAuthorize("...")`** — Evaluated before method execution. Has access to method parameters and the `authentication` object for security checks.

**4. `@ConditionalOnExpression("...")`** — Evaluated once during context refresh for conditional bean registration.

**5. `@EventListener(condition = "...")`** — Evaluated on each event. The event object is the root, so `#root.orderId` accesses event properties.

**6. Spring Data `@Query` with SpEL** — `?#{principal.username}` injects the authenticated user into a JPA query.

The most important thing to remember: SpEL errors are **runtime errors**, not compile-time errors. A typo in a SpEL expression compiles fine and fails when the expression is first evaluated — which might be on the first request, not at startup. Keep expressions simple, and test beans with SpEL annotations early.

questions.title: Meta-Annotations and Composed Annotations
questions.question: What are meta-annotations and composed annotations in Spring?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- **Meta-annotation:** an annotation on an annotation
- **Composed annotation:** a new annotation that combines multiple annotations into one
- **Examples:** `@RestController` = `@Controller` + `@ResponseBody`
- **`@AliasFor`:** creates aliases between attributes in composed annotations
- **Red flag:** not knowing `@RestController`, `@SpringBootApplication`, `@GetMapping` are all composed annotations

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
A meta-annotation is an annotation that's applied to another annotation definition. A composed annotation is a custom annotation that brings together multiple existing annotations into one.

Spring uses composed annotations extensively. `@RestController` is `@Controller` + `@ResponseBody`. `@GetMapping` is `@RequestMapping(method = RequestMethod.GET)`. `@SpringBootApplication` is `@EnableAutoConfiguration` + `@ComponentScan` + `@Configuration`. These reduce boilerplate and express intent more clearly.

You can create your own composed annotations. If you always use `@Service` + `@Transactional` together, create a `@TransactionalService` annotation that includes both. Spring's annotation processing understands meta-annotations and processes them as if the original annotations were present.

sections.title: The Composition Pattern That Makes @SpringBootApplication Possible
sections.content:
When you write `@SpringBootApplication` on your main class, you're applying **three annotations in one**: `@SpringBootConfiguration` (which includes `@Configuration`), `@EnableAutoConfiguration`, and `@ComponentScan`. This composition works because Spring supports **meta-annotations** — annotations that are themselves annotated with other annotations. Spring detects the presence of annotations at any depth in the hierarchy.

This isn't a Spring-specific Java feature — it's a Spring convention built on top of Java's annotation system. Java's `@Inherited` annotation only handles class-level inheritance, and Java doesn't natively walk annotation hierarchies. Spring's `AnnotationUtils` and `MergedAnnotations` API do this custom scanning, checking each annotation for annotations on itself, recursively.

The practical value of meta-annotations is **reducing boilerplate and enforcing conventions**. Instead of writing `@Service @Transactional @Validated @Scope("request")` on every request-scoped service, you create a `@RequestScopedService` composed annotation that bundles all four. Every new service gets consistent configuration with one annotation, and changing the convention (adding `@Cacheable`, modifying the scope) updates one annotation definition — not fifty service classes.

Custom composed annotations are especially valuable for teams with coding standards. A `@SecureEndpoint` annotation that combines `@RestController`, `@PreAuthorize("isAuthenticated()")`, and `@CrossOrigin` ensures every secured controller gets the same security configuration without relying on developers remembering to add all three annotations.

questions.title: Auto-Configuration Mechanism
questions.question: How does Spring Boot's auto-configuration mechanism work internally?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- **`@EnableAutoConfiguration` → reads `META-INF/spring/auto-configuration`**
- **Auto-configuration classes use `@Conditional*` to decide what to configure**
- **You override by declaring your own beans:** `@ConditionalOnMissingBean` allows this
- **Spring Boot 2.7+:** `META-INF/spring/org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.AutoConfiguration.imports`
- **Red flag:** thinking auto-configuration is magic — it's just `@Conditional` beans with a discovery mechanism

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
Spring Boot's auto-configuration is built on two mechanisms: a discovery file that lists all auto-configuration classes, and `@Conditional` annotations that decide whether each configuration actually applies.

When `@EnableAutoConfiguration` is activated — which `@SpringBootApplication` includes — Spring Boot reads `META-INF/spring/org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.AutoConfiguration.imports`. This file, shipped inside Spring Boot's JARs, lists hundreds of auto-configuration classes like `DataSourceAutoConfiguration`, `JpaAutoConfiguration`, and `RedisAutoConfiguration`.

Each auto-configuration class is annotated with conditions. `DataSourceAutoConfiguration` is annotated with `@ConditionalOnClass(DataSource.class)` — it only runs if a JDBC driver is on the classpath. `@ConditionalOnMissingBean(DataSource.class)` means it skips configuration if you've already defined a `DataSource`. This is the escape hatch: declare your own bean and the auto-configuration backs off.

sections.title: The Conditional Loading Mechanism That Makes Spring Boot 'Just Work'
sections.content:
Spring Boot's auto-configuration is the mechanism behind the "add a dependency, get a working configuration" experience. When you add `spring-boot-starter-data-jpa` to your project, you get a `DataSource`, an `EntityManagerFactory`, a `TransactionManager`, and JPA repositories — all without writing a single `@Bean` method. Understanding how this works internally is the difference between blindly trusting the magic and being able to debug it when it breaks.

The mechanism has four moving parts: **discovery** (Spring Boot finds auto-configuration classes), **condition evaluation** (each class checks whether it should activate), **bean creation** (activated classes create beans with `@ConditionalOnMissingBean`), and **ordering** (auto-configuration runs after user-defined configuration).

Discovery uses the file `META-INF/spring/org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.AutoConfiguration.imports`, where each line is a fully-qualified auto-configuration class name. Spring Boot reads this file from every JAR on the classpath, collecting all auto-configuration candidates. The `spring-boot-autoconfigure` JAR alone contains over 150 auto-configuration classes.

The key insight is that most of these classes are **not activated**. Each one is guarded by `@ConditionalOnClass`, `@ConditionalOnProperty`, or other condition annotations. `HibernateJpaAutoConfiguration` only activates if Hibernate is on the classpath. `RedisAutoConfiguration` only activates if the Redis client library is present. This conditional evaluation means auto-configuration is a whitelist, not a blanket — only the configurations relevant to your dependencies are activated.

sections.title: The Condition Evaluation Pipeline: How Spring Decides What to Activate
sections.content:
During context refresh, Spring Boot evaluates conditions on each auto-configuration class in two passes: a **filter pass** and a **full evaluation pass**.

The filter pass uses `AutoConfigurationImportFilter` to quickly eliminate candidates based on `@ConditionalOnClass`. This pass reads bytecode metadata (not class loading) to check if the required class exists. It's an optimization — checking 150 classes for classpath conditions is faster with bytecode scanning than with full class loading and reflection.

The full evaluation pass processes remaining classes through the standard `Condition` interface. `@ConditionalOnProperty` checks the `Environment`, `@ConditionalOnBean` and `@ConditionalOnMissingBean` check the bean registry, and custom `Condition` implementations run arbitrary logic.

The evaluation order matters for `@ConditionalOnBean` and `@ConditionalOnMissingBean`. Auto-configuration classes are processed **after** user-defined `@Configuration` classes. This ordering is guaranteed by `@AutoConfiguration` (or the older `@AutoConfigureAfter`/`@AutoConfigureBefore` annotations). Because user configurations run first, their beans are already registered by the time auto-configuration evaluates `@ConditionalOnMissingBean`.

To debug which conditions passed or failed, set `debug=true` in your application properties or visit `/actuator/conditions`. Spring Boot produces a detailed report showing every auto-configuration class, which conditions were evaluated, which passed, and which caused the class to be excluded. This report is the fastest way to answer "why isn't X auto-configured?" or "why is the default bean being used instead of mine?"

sections.title: Reading the Auto-Configuration Debug Report
sections.content:
The conditions report (`debug=true` or `/actuator/conditions`) is the primary debugging tool for auto-configuration issues. Here's how to read it.

```
Positive matches:
-----------------
DataSourceAutoConfiguration matched:
  - @ConditionalOnClass found required classes 'javax.sql.DataSource',
    'org.springframework.jdbc.datasource.embedded.EmbeddedDatabaseType'

DataSourceAutoConfiguration.PooledDataSourceConfiguration matched:
  - @ConditionalOnMissingBean DataSource found no beans

Negative matches:
-----------------
RedisAutoConfiguration:
  Did not match:
    - @ConditionalOnClass did not find required class
      'org.springframework.data.redis.core.RedisOperations'

JpaRepositoriesAutoConfiguration:
  Did not match:
    - @ConditionalOnMissingBean DataSource found bean 'dataSource'
```

**Positive matches** tell you what activated and why. `DataSourceAutoConfiguration` activated because the JDBC classes were on the classpath and no user-defined `DataSource` bean existed.

**Negative matches** tell you what was skipped. `RedisAutoConfiguration` was skipped because the Redis library isn't on the classpath — expected behavior if you're not using Redis. But `JpaRepositoriesAutoConfiguration` was skipped because a `DataSource` bean already existed — this might indicate a conflict.

The most common debugging scenario is "my custom bean isn't being used." Check the positive matches for the auto-configured bean. If it shows `@ConditionalOnMissingBean found no beans`, your custom bean wasn't registered before the auto-configuration evaluated — typically because your `@Configuration` class isn't being component-scanned. Verify the package hierarchy and component scan base packages.

questions.title: IoC Container Internals
questions.question: How does Spring's IoC container manage bean dependencies internally?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- **`DefaultListableBeanFactory`:** the core IoC implementation
- **Dependency graph resolution:** topological sort of bean dependencies
- **Three-level cache for circular reference resolution** (for setter/field injection only)
- **`ObjectFactory`:** deferred lookup pattern for breaking circular dependencies
- **Red flag:** not knowing Spring builds a dependency graph — thinking it's just sequential

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
The core of Spring's IoC container is `DefaultListableBeanFactory`. When you call `getBean(name)`, or when `finishBeanFactoryInitialization` eagerly creates singleton beans, the factory does a topological sort of the dependency graph — it resolves A before B if B depends on A.

For constructor injection, the graph must be acyclic — circular dependencies fail immediately because Spring can't construct either bean without the other already existing.

For setter/field injection, Spring uses a three-level cache to handle circular dependencies. When creating bean A, Spring puts an `ObjectFactory` for A into the third-level cache ('singletonFactories'). When B is being created and needs A, Spring uses this factory to get an early reference to A's partially-constructed object. This breaks the circle, but it means B holds a reference to an incompletely initialized A — which is why Spring 2.6+ disallows it by default.

The three-level cache is an internal implementation detail, but interviewers ask about it to probe deep Spring knowledge.

sections.title: The Dependency Graph That Determines Bean Creation Order
sections.content:
Spring's IoC (Inversion of Control) container is fundamentally a **dependency graph resolver**. When the application starts, the container collects all bean definitions, constructs a directed acyclic graph (DAG) of dependencies between them, and creates beans in topological order — dependencies first, dependents second. Understanding this graph explains every startup ordering behavior, every circular dependency error, and every "bean not found" message.

The process starts with all bean definitions loaded into the `BeanDefinitionRegistry`. Each definition describes what a bean needs — its constructor parameters, its injected fields, its `@DependsOn` declarations. The container builds the dependency graph from this metadata: if `OrderService` requires `UserRepository` in its constructor, there's an edge from `OrderService` to `UserRepository`. `UserRepository` must be created first.

For constructor injection, dependencies are explicit in the definition — they're constructor parameters. For field and setter injection, the dependencies are discovered later, during `AutowiredAnnotationBeanPostProcessor` execution. This means field injection dependencies are **invisible** to the initial graph construction. The container discovers them just-in-time during bean creation, which is why circular dependencies with field injection historically didn't cause startup failures (though Spring Boot 2.6+ prohibits them by default).

The container resolves the graph using depth-first creation. When creating `OrderService`, it encounters the `UserRepository` dependency. If `UserRepository` isn't created yet, the container pauses `OrderService` creation, creates `UserRepository` (and its dependencies recursively), then resumes `OrderService`. The "currently in creation" tracking detects cycles: if creating `UserRepository` leads back to `OrderService`, the container throws `BeanCurrentlyInCreationException`.

sections.title: The Three-Level Singleton Cache: How Spring Handles Circular References
sections.content:
Spring's singleton registry uses three maps — the **three-level cache** — to manage bean creation and (historically) allow circular references with field/setter injection.

**Level 1: `singletonObjects`** — The fully initialized bean cache. Beans here have completed all lifecycle phases: construction, injection, `@PostConstruct`, and post-processor wrapping. This is where `getBean()` looks first.

**Level 2: `earlySingletonObjects`** — Partially initialized beans exposed early to break circular references. The bean has been constructed but hasn't completed injection or initialization.

**Level 3: `singletonFactories`** — Factory callbacks that can create early references. When a bean supports AOP proxying, the factory creates the proxy early so that other beans get the proxy reference (not the raw instance) even during circular resolution.

The resolution flow: Bean A is being created. The container registers a factory for A in Level 3. A's dependency B is created next. B depends on A. The container finds A's factory in Level 3, calls it to get an early reference, moves it to Level 2, and injects it into B. B completes initialization. Back in A's creation, A completes initialization and moves from Level 2 to Level 1.

Since Spring Boot 2.6, this mechanism is disabled by default (`spring.main.allow-circular-references=false`). The three-level cache still exists (for AOP proxy creation), but circular reference resolution through it is blocked. The rationale: circular dependencies are design problems, and silently resolving them through early references masks issues that should be fixed structurally.

questions.title: Spring Boot Startup Sequence
questions.question: What happens internally when a Spring Boot application starts?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- **`SpringApplication.run()` is the entry point:** not just calling `main()`
- **Key phases:** create context, load auto-configurations, refresh context (create beans), start embedded server
- **`SpringApplicationRunListener`:** hooks into each startup phase
- **`ApplicationRunner` / `CommandLineRunner`:** run code after context is ready
- **Red flag:** not knowing the refresh phase is where beans are actually created

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
Spring Boot's startup begins at `SpringApplication.run()`. It determines the application type — Servlet-based, Reactive, or non-web — and creates the appropriate `ConfigurableApplicationContext`. It loads the environment and property sources, then broadcasts `ApplicationStartingEvent` to any registered listeners.

The context is then prepared: the application class is registered as a bean definition, and `ApplicationContextInitializer` implementations run. Then the context is refreshed — this is the major step where all bean definitions are loaded, `BeanFactoryPostProcessor` runs, `BeanPostProcessor` runs, all singleton beans are instantiated, and the embedded server starts.

After refresh, `ApplicationStartedEvent` fires, then `ApplicationRunner` and `CommandLineRunner` beans run in order, and finally `ApplicationReadyEvent` fires — at this point the application is fully ready to serve traffic.

sections.title: From main() to 'Started Application': The 7 Phases of Spring Boot Startup
sections.content:
When `SpringApplication.run(Application.class, args)` executes, it triggers a precise multi-phase startup process. Each phase has a specific purpose, and startup errors map directly to the phase that failed. Understanding these phases turns "application won't start" from a mystery into a diagnostic exercise.

The phases are: **SpringApplication construction** (determine app type, load spring.factories), **Environment preparation** (resolve properties and profiles), **ApplicationContext creation** (choose the right context type), **Context preparation** (register beans, apply initializers), **Context refresh** (the core startup — scan, process, instantiate), **Runner execution** (CommandLineRunner, ApplicationRunner), and **Event publication** (signal readiness to the world).

The startup process is observable through `SpringApplicationRunListener`, which publishes events at each phase boundary. Spring Boot logs phase transitions at INFO level — the familiar "Started Application in X seconds" message — but the events carry much more detail. Custom listeners can add monitoring, tracing, or conditional behavior at each phase.

Understanding that the context refresh (phase 5) is where most of the work happens is critical. All bean scanning, condition evaluation, definition registration, post-processor execution, and singleton instantiation happens inside `AbstractApplicationContext.refresh()`. This single method call accounts for 80-90% of startup time in typical applications. If your startup is slow, the bottleneck is almost certainly inside refresh — a bean with an expensive constructor, a component scan covering too many packages, or an auto-configuration that loads a large resource.

sections.title: Phases 1-3: Before Any Beans Exist
sections.content:
**Phase 1 — SpringApplication construction:** The `SpringApplication` constructor detects the application type (servlet, reactive, or none) by checking the classpath for `DispatcherServlet` and `DispatcherHandler`. It loads `spring.factories` to discover `ApplicationContextInitializer` and `SpringApplicationRunListener` implementations. No beans exist yet.

**Phase 2 — Environment preparation:** `SpringApplicationRunListeners.environmentPrepared()` fires. Spring creates the `Environment` object and populates it with property sources: system properties, environment variables, command-line arguments, `application.properties`/`application.yml`, and profile-specific files. Active profiles are resolved from the `spring.profiles.active` property.

This is where `application-{profile}.properties` files are loaded. If your application fails with "Could not resolve placeholder" errors, the problem is in this phase — the property source that should contain the value isn't being loaded (wrong profile, wrong file name, wrong location).

**Phase 3 — Context creation:** Based on the detected application type, Spring Boot creates the appropriate `ApplicationContext` subclass: `AnnotationConfigServletWebServerApplicationContext` for servlet apps, `AnnotationConfigReactiveWebServerApplicationContext` for reactive apps, or `AnnotationConfigApplicationContext` for non-web apps. The context is created but empty — no beans are registered yet.

`ApplicationContextInitializers` run at this point, providing a hook to modify the context before any beans are loaded. This is used internally for things like adding property sources from Spring Cloud Config, but application developers rarely need it.
